newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns Russia of retaliation in spy case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Russia of retaliation in spy case.

text.p: The United States has protested to Russia over the activities of a CIA officer charged with selling secrets to Moscow and has threatened retaliation, the State Department said on Tuesday.

Calling the incident "unacceptable," spokesman Glyn Davies said protests had been lodged in Washington and Moscow following Saturday's arrest by U.S. authorities of Harold Nicholson, a 16-year Central Intelligence Agency veteran.

Davies told reporters Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott called in Russian Ambassador Yuli Vorontsov on Monday and the U.S. Embassy delivered a similar demarche in Moscow. "The message of course was that we view this activity as unacceptable and we reserve the right to take further action."

Davies said Washington saw the incident as "inconsistent with the pattern of bilateral relations of recent years. We have demanded an explanation ... and made clear that we are considering appropriate measures."

He declined to speculate on what steps the United States might take but other officials said they were likely to be in line with action in past similar cases. That raised the possibility of an expulsion, perhaps of an agent of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service working under diplomatic cover at the Russian Embassy in Washington.
In Moscow, Foreign Ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin said Russia viewed the incident as an internal matter of the United States "and we have nothing to do with it."

Nicholson, 46, was a clandestine operations officer who was CIA station chief in Romania and deputy chief of station in Malaysia before becoming a CIA instructor in intelligence skills. His most recent job was as a branch chief in the CIA's Counter-Terrorism Centre.

The government alleged at a court hearing on Monday that for the past two years he gave Moscow information identifying U.S. spies about to be sent abroad, among other secrets, in exchange for cash payments totalling at least $120,000.

CIA Director John Deutch said on Tuesday he would back a government decision not to seek the death penalty if Nicholson is convicted. "That's a decision for the prosecutor and I would stand with the prosecutor's decision," Deutch said on the NBC "Today" programme.

Prosecutors on Monday said Nicholson, the highest-ranking CIA officer ever charged with spying, faced life imprisonment without possibility of parole if convicted on the basis of the evidence they now have.

There were signs that by its strong diplomatic action Washington was seeking to regain the moral high ground after an embarrassing incident in which U.S. authorities arrested, and then released, a former Soviet KGB spy.

Vladimir Galkin, who had given full details of his previous employment on his U.S. visa application, was arrested on Oct. 29 and accused of trying to obtain secret information on the U.S. "Star Wars" missile defence programme in 1991.

Moscow threatened retaliatory measures, saying the United States had violated an unwritten code allowing retired agents to travel freely. Washington freed Galkin after the personal intervention of Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
